added_claim_errors: "roughly $1,220-$1,240" forfeited: the $1,240 end uses the 2025 cap of $660; for 2026 it is $1,220 (minor, hedged with "roughly")
"Unused carryover still expires later": imprecise, since carried money can itself carry over again up to the cap and only the excess is forfeited (minor)

"the carryover only happens if you're still employed and still enrolled in the FSA in the new plan year": the job-loss part is right, but "still enrolled" is stated as fact when it is plan-dependent and unverified
"you usually have until March-April to submit receipts": typical run-out range, unverifiable as a general claim
The "realistic math" table treats ~$680 carried and ~$1,220 forfeited as the baseline before the grace-period caveat, which could read as near-certain loss (softened by the next paragraph)

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start, give the right $680 cap for 2026 (and $660 for 2025), say a plan has carryover or a grace period but not both, and send the person to HR with the right questions. A also gives explicit branch rules (spend at least $1,900 minus the cap; grace period through about March 15, and after that treat the money as use-it-or-lose-it). Unlike B, A states plainly that prepaying for March work does not help because the expense counts on the date of service (key point 6). B only implies this by moving the work into December. B has the fuller list of eligible spend-down items (key point 7) and spells out that run-out only extends filing time. It is longer, with padding such as the junk-purchase trap and a disclaimer. Neither mentions the 2027 open-enrollment election (key point 8). A is tighter and covers more of the key's decision points; B is stronger only on the spend-down list.
